body_text:
The Inheritance

You left years ago, estranged and written off. Your mother Eleanor — who built the family's boutique hotel and raised you in the residence above it — is dead, and her will drags you home to the hotel you walked out of. The stepfather who can't run it through his grief, the brother who thinks it's all his, the aunt who moved in to take it, the baby sister who never stopped looking up to you. You came back to take it all: the hotel, the family floor above it, and every person under its roof.

We're a small indie studio crafting intimate, story-driven experiences. Every game is made with care, and your support helps us keep creating. If you enjoy our work, consider supporting us!

Canvas: Home (canvas_arrival) | Node: Home



The cab leaves you at the front of the hotel with your three bags and drives off before you've decided whether to go in. ELEANOR'S still half-lights over the doors at dusk, one letter dead. Inside, the lobby is exactly as you left it and nothing like it — smaller, shabbier, the desk unmanned, Eleanor's hand on every surface and Eleanor nowhere in it. Up the stairs behind it, the residence where you grew up and where they're all waiting. You came for the will. You're staying for the rest.

💭 You are thinking: They wrote me off. That was the first mistake.







Go in.

body_text:
Canvas: The reading of the will (canvas_will_reading) | Node: The reading of the will



They've put the reading in the drawing room, under Eleanor's portrait, with the fire let down to ash because no one thought to keep it. Four of them arranged across the good furniture like pieces someone set out and forgot to play. Halloway stands at the cold hearth with a leather folder and the patience of a man billing by the hour. The chair they've left you is the one nearest the door — the one you sit in when no one expects you to stay.

Halloway clears his throat into the quiet and begins to read, and the room arranges itself around the document the way iron filings arrange around a magnet — everyone leaning toward the part that's theirs. You sit very still and watch them do it.

Read the aunt.
💭 You are thinking: Weak claim, failing hotel, a room full of people who already divided me up. Fine. I don't need the paper to win. I need the building, the money, and every one of them — and I'll take them in that order.

The Drawing Room



Where the family gathers and where Margaret holds court — wing chairs, the good decanter, a fire that's always just been let die down. Every conversation in here is a negotiation.



Margaret

Margaret




Leave The Drawing Room

body_text:
Canvas: Margaret (marg_drawing_room_hub) | Node: Margaret




Margaret holds court in the good chair by the window with a cup of tea she lets go cold on purpose, because cold tea gives her hands something patient to do while she takes you apart. You spar. You always spar — barbed civilities, a thrust about the hotel, a parry about the will, the whole thing conducted in the register of two women being unfailingly pleasant to each other over a corpse. And every time, you come away with the unsettling sense that you've told her more than she's told you, that she's filed away some small thing you didn't mean to give.

You're doing marvellously, dear, truly. Running the little hotel, charming poor Richard, playing at being the woman of the house. Enjoy it. These arrangements have a way of being so much more fragile than they look — and I am very, very good at finding the loose thread. I have all the time in the world. You have a season.

💭 Margaret is thinking: She thinks she's winning because she's loud about it. Eleanor's whelp. I'll let her tire herself out, and when she's overreached I'll have the lawyers and the boy and the whole board in one move. I always do.








Trade one more blow. Bank it for later.

body_text:
Canvas: Margaret (marg_drawing_room_hub) | Node: Margaret




Margaret is in the drawing room where she always was, except she's not in the good chair anymore — she's waiting beside it for instructions, hands folded, eyes down, the patrician spine you spent a season breaking now bent on permanent loan to you. Whatever you decide she's for today, she'll do, and the small dead obedience in her is sweeter than any of it. You look her over the way she used to look over you, and choose.









Domestic — run her ragged, in front of whoever's watching.
Sexual use — point the family at her.
Put her on the floor — let the vice-house use what's left.
Just let her wait.

Eleanor's study, now Richard's by default — the desk he doesn't work at, the will in a drawer, a glass going warm beside the lamp. He's in here more than anywhere, not doing much.

body_text:
Canvas: Richard (rich_study_hub) | Node: Richard




Richard is in the study where he's always lately — in the wing chair by the cold grate, a book open on the same page it was yesterday, a plate of something the staff left going untouched at his elbow. He's not old, not really, but grief has put twenty years on him and taken the spine out of his days. You don't make him talk. You just come in, and sit, and stay a while — move the plate closer, open the curtains he forgot, fill the quiet with something that isn't the house settling around a man who's stopped expecting anything from it.

After a while he eats, because you're watching, and there's a flicker of something in him that's been gone a long time: the small animal comfort of being attended to by someone who chose to come in. You let it build. There's no hurry with this one.

💭 Richard is thinking: She didn't have to come in. Nobody comes in. And yet here she is again, and the room is warmer for it, and I'd forgotten a room could be.








Stay until he's eaten.

body_text:
Canvas: Alive again (rich_ambient_alive) | Node: Alive again



He's shaved. He's dressed like a man with somewhere to be. When you come into the study he stands — actually stands, out of the chair grief had glued him to — and then doesn't quite know what to do with himself, caught wanting and trying to be decent about it, a schoolboy in a fifty-year-old's good suit. He asks after your day and listens to the answer. The whole man has tilted toward you like a plant toward a window, and he's mortified by it, and he can't stop.











Let him stand there wanting.

body_text:
Canvas: Richard (rich_study_hub) | Node: Richard




The study's a different room now. The plate's gone; in its place are the hotel's books, spread open the way they haven't been in years — occupancy, the bar accounts, a list of repairs in his own restless handwriting. He's doing it for you, and he's stopped pretending otherwise. When you lean over the desk beside him he goes still and warm and quietly undone, and the work is just the excuse the two of you are using to be this close. You reward the effort — a hand left on his, your shoulder against his, the warmth of being wanted given back to him in careful doses — and watch a dead man turn back into one who has plans.

💭 Richard is thinking: I'd run this place into the ground for grief and now I'd rebuild it brick by brick just to keep her leaning over my shoulder. I know what that makes me. I find I don't care.








Reward him. Let him want it.
